\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity necessarily carries a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 0.5--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning; rates correlate with schema restrictiveness (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology or model scale.
At deployment-grade quality (R-F1 40--46\%), even 1--2\% residual violations compound across thousands of documents into systematic knowledge graph corruption, making reliable constraint enforcement necessary.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} ensures syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering improves precision but discards up to 48\% of predictions including true positives; at high rejection rates (e.g., Mistral DocRED 73.7\%), it becomes impractical.
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} internalize schema knowledge but provide only soft guidance without runtime enforcement; no method provides both semantic awareness and hard constraint enforcement.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that translates IE ontologies into composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
A decidability analysis of IE type constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability}) yields a two-layer architecture: the \emph{grammar layer} compiles ontology constraints into context-free grammars (JSON structure, vocabulary membership) via XGrammar; the \emph{semantic layer} interprets type constraints at runtime via dynamic logit masking over an entity registry, with an \emph{empirical enabling dependency} between layers.
OntoCoDec compiles constraints automatically from IE ontologies, requires no constraint-specific training, and is applicable to autoregressive LMs with logits access; we validate on three English datasets (up to 96 relation types), five models (7--70B), and three tokenizer families (Llama, Qwen, Mistral).
DR enforcement is precision-preserving but introduces CF side-effects (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}); fine-tuning resolves most CF ($\leq$1.3\%).
LoRA + greedy S1 near-eliminates DR ($\leq$0.09\%) with R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp and $+$10\% latency; beam S1 ($k{=}4$) eliminates DR on both datasets (1.54$\times$ latency).
Zero-shot evaluation on 7--8B models with preliminary 70B results confirms DR drops by 76--99\% for models with well-calibrated type predictions (excluding Mistral-7B due to atypical entity typing interaction; \S\ref{sec:cross-model}).

We make a systematic engineering contribution with theoretical grounding:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
    \item A two-layer constrained decoding framework: we formalize a well-known intuition that cross-field type constraints require runtime state beyond context-free expressiveness (Proposition~1), yielding pair-based sequential enforcement at each level (\S\ref{sec:decidability}). Constraints compile automatically from IE ontologies, validated on schemas of varying restrictiveness with up to 96 relation types.
    \item A comprehensive evaluation of type constraint enforcement across 3 IE datasets, 5 models (7--70B), and 2 tasks: (a)~for RE, the five-way ablation confirms that neither layer alone achieves $>$24\% DR reduction while their composition yields 92--100\% DR reduction in fine-tuned settings; zero-shot effectiveness is dataset-dependent (45--99\%), with entity type errors accounting for most residual DR in complex schemas (\S\ref{sec:docred-results}); (b)~event extraction results on WikiEvents provide initial evidence for applicability beyond RE, covering 245 constraints across three tokenizer families (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}).
\end{enumerate}

We present \textsc{OntoCoDec}, a framework that translates Information Extraction (IE) ontologies into composable token-level decoding constraints via a decidability-guided architecture: a \emph{grammar layer} (context-free) compiles ontology constraints into grammars ensuring JSON validity and vocabulary membership; a \emph{semantic layer} (prefix-decidable with state) interprets type constraints at runtime via stateful token masking over a dynamic entity registry, with grammar-first fallback when constraints conflict.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity necessarily carries a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 0.5--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning; rates correlate with schema restrictiveness (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology or model scale.
At deployment-grade quality (R-F1 40--46\%), even 1--2\% residual violations compound across thousands of documents into systematic knowledge graph corruption, making reliable constraint enforcement necessary.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} ensures syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering improves precision but discards up to 48\% of predictions including true positives; at high rejection rates (e.g., Mistral DocRED 73.7\%), it becomes impractical.
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} internalize schema knowledge but provide only soft guidance without runtime enforcement; no method provides both semantic awareness and hard constraint enforcement.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that translates IE ontologies into composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
A decidability analysis of IE type constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability}) yields a two-layer architecture: the \emph{grammar layer} compiles ontology constraints into context-free grammars (JSON structure, vocabulary membership) via XGrammar; the \emph{semantic layer} interprets type constraints at runtime via dynamic logit masking over an entity registry, with an \emph{empirical enabling dependency} between layers.
OntoCoDec compiles constraints automatically from IE ontologies, requires no constraint-specific training, and is applicable to autoregressive LMs with logits access; we validate on three English datasets (up to 96 relation types), five models (7--70B), and three tokenizer families (Llama, Qwen, Mistral).
DR enforcement is precision-preserving but introduces CF side-effects (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}); fine-tuning resolves most CF ($\leq$1.3\%).
LoRA + greedy S1 near-eliminates DR ($\leq$0.09\%) with R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp and $+$10\% latency; beam S1 ($k{=}4$) eliminates DR on both datasets (1.54$\times$ latency).
Zero-shot evaluation on 7--8B models with preliminary 70B results confirms DR drops by 76--99\% for models with well-calibrated type predictions (excluding Mistral-7B due to atypical entity typing interaction; \S\ref{sec:cross-model}).

We make a systematic engineering contribution with theoretical grounding:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
    \item A two-layer constrained decoding framework: we formalize a well-known intuition that cross-field type constraints require runtime state beyond context-free expressiveness (Proposition~1), yielding pair-based sequential enforcement at each level (\S\ref{sec:decidability}). Constraints compile automatically from IE ontologies, validated on schemas of varying restrictiveness with up to 96 relation types.
    \item A comprehensive evaluation of type constraint enforcement across 3 IE datasets, 5 models (7--70B), and 2 tasks: (a)~for RE, the five-way ablation confirms that neither layer alone achieves $>$24\% DR reduction while their composition yields 92--100\% DR reduction in fine-tuned settings; zero-shot effectiveness is dataset-dependent (45--99\%), with entity type errors accounting for most residual DR in complex schemas (\S\ref{sec:docred-results}); (b)~event extraction results on WikiEvents provide initial evidence for applicability beyond RE, covering 245 constraints across three tokenizer families (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Reproducibility Details}
\label{app:reproducibility}

\paragraph{Fine-tuning configuration.}
All four fine-tuned models (Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on SciERC and DocRED) use identical LoRA hyperparameters: rank $r{=}16$, $\alpha{=}32$, dropout $0.05$, no bias, targeting all attention and MLP projection layers (\texttt{q\_proj}, \texttt{k\_proj}, \texttt{v\_proj}, \texttt{o\_proj}, \texttt{gate\_proj}, \texttt{up\_proj}, \texttt{down\_proj}).
Training uses AdamW with learning rate $2{\times}10^{-4}$, cosine schedule, warmup ratio $0.1$, effective batch size $16$, bf16 precision, gradient checkpointing, and completion-only loss for 3 epochs.
SciERC trains on 1,762 examples (260 dev) for 333 steps; DocRED trains on 3,053 examples (998 dev) for 573 steps.
Maximum sequence length is 2,048 (SciERC) and 4,096 (DocRED).
All runs use seed 42.

\paragraph{Hardware and software.}
Training runs on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU (98\,GB VRAM).
SciERC fine-tuning takes approximately 11 minutes per model; DocRED takes approximately 1.5 hours.
Software versions: PyTorch 2.10, Transformers 4.57, PEFT 0.19, TRL 1.1, Accelerate 1.13.

\paragraph{Inference time.}
Inference timing is reported in Appendix~\ref{app:runtime} (NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU, same hardware as training).
Full S1 constrained decoding adds $+$13.1\% wall-clock overhead on SciERC and $+$2.43\% on DocRED (Qwen3-8B, zero-shot greedy); under LoRA fine-tuning, overhead is $+$10.0\% on SciERC.

\paragraph{Greedy decoding determinism.}
\label{app:greedy-determinism}
% exp_id: d067_seed_variance
All main results use greedy decoding (temperature$\,{=}\,$0, argmax token selection).
Argmax is deterministic: the random seed controls \texttt{torch.manual\_seed} for sampling and dropout, neither of which is active during greedy inference.
We verify this with three seeds (42, 123, 456) across two LoRA fine-tuned models on all 551 SciERC documents.
Seeds 123 and 456, evaluated on the same GPU, produce byte-identical outputs for both Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B.
The residual variance in Table~\ref{tab:seed-variance} stems entirely from cross-hardware floating-point divergence: seed 42 was evaluated on a different server with a different CUDA driver version.
Even under this conservative upper bound, $\sigma(\text{E-F1}) \leq 0.16$\,pp, $\sigma(\text{R-F1}) \leq 0.43$\,pp, and $\sigma(\text{DR\%}) \leq 0.08$\,pp.
The constrained decoding DR\% reduction ($-$2.06\,pp for Qwen, $-$1.01\,pp for Llama) exceeds this variance by ${>}12\times$ (signal-to-noise ratio ${>}$\,12), confirming that observed improvements reflect genuine method effects rather than run-to-run noise.
We therefore report single-run results without error bars; bootstrap confidence intervals (10{,}000 iterations) are provided for F1 metrics.
